questions.q: Where do fetch, localStorage and document come from?
questions.explain: The language defines values, functions and built-ins like JSON. Everything that touches the outside world comes from the host. Node.js is a different host that implements some of the same Web APIs (fetch, URL) and not others (document, localStorage).
options: They are part of the JavaScript language, defined by ECMAScript
The host environment (the browser) provides them as Web APIs, defined by web standards
They are npm packages the browser installs
Node.js provides them to the browser

questions.q: Your page uses the Clipboard API when it exists. What is the reliable way to decide?
questions.explain: Feature detection asks about the feature itself. Browser names in the user-agent string are unreliable and say nothing about which features a given version has, or whether the page is in a secure context where the API is allowed.
options: Check whether it exists, for example "clipboard" in navigator, and fall back if not
Try it and let the page crash if it is missing
Only support the newest version of one browser

questions.q: When does the promise returned by fetch(url) reject?
questions.explain: A 404 or 500 is still a response, so fetch fulfils. Check response.ok. Invalid JSON makes response.json() reject, which is a separate promise.
options: When the status is 400 or higher
When the status is 500 or higher
Only when no HTTP response arrived: network down, server unreachable, request blocked or aborted
When the body is not valid JSON

questions.q: What does response.ok tell you?
questions.explain: ok is only a status check. A 201 is ok; a 304, 404 or 500 is not. The body may still be anything.
options: That the body is valid JSON
That the status is in the range 200 to 299
That the request did not time out
That the server set a Content-Type header

questions.q: A logging helper calls await response.text() to record the reply, and then the caller calls await response.json(). What happens, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: A response body is consumed by reading it (bodyUsed becomes true). response.clone() before the first read gives a second, independent body.
options: Both work; the body is cached
The second read throws because a body is a stream that can be read once; read it once and share the value, or clone() the response first
The second read returns an empty object

questions.q: Where should a web app keep a user's login session?
questions.explain: Any script on the page can read localStorage and sessionStorage, including an attacker's injected script. An HttpOnly cookie is sent with requests but is invisible to JavaScript.
options: In a cookie the server sets with HttpOnly, which the page's JavaScript cannot read at all

questions.q: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
questions.explain: Both store strings with the same methods. They differ in lifetime and scope. Neither is sent to the server; cookies are.
options: localStorage lasts until it is deleted and is shared by all tabs of the origin; sessionStorage belongs to one tab and ends with it
sessionStorage is sent to the server with every request

questions.q: A page calls localStorage.setItem("cart", …). Which pages receive a storage event?
questions.explain: The event exists to keep other tabs in step. The page that wrote the value already knows about it.
options: Only the page that made the change
Every other open page of the same origin, but not the page that made the change
Every open page of every site
No page; the event only fires after a reload

questions.q: A widget's reset button calls localStorage.clear(). Why is that a bad idea on most sites?
questions.explain: All scripts on an origin share one storage. Prefix your keys ("tasks-app:") and remove only your own.
options: It deletes every key of the origin, including data other scripts on the same site stored (settings, progress, drafts)
clear() is asynchronous and may not finish

questions.q: Why should code validate what it reads from localStorage, even though only your own code wrote it?
questions.explain: Stored data outlives the code that wrote it and is editable in developer tools. Treat it like any input: parse inside try, check the shape and version, and fall back to a default.
options: The data may have been written by an older version of your app, edited by the user, or corrupted, so its shape is not guaranteed

questions.q: What happens when localStorage.setItem would exceed the origin's quota?
questions.explain: Storage writes can throw (quota, disabled storage). An uncaught throw at start-up or in a save handler breaks the page, so wrap writes and keep working in memory.
options: The oldest keys are deleted to make room
The value is silently cut short
It throws a QuotaExceededError, which your code must catch
The browser asks the user for more space

questions.q: A single-page app calls history.pushState(null, "", "/tasks/7") when a task is opened, and renders the task. The user presses Back: the address changes to /tasks, but the page still shows task 7. What is missing?
questions.explain: The History API only manages entries and the address bar. On Back and Forward the browser fires popstate, and your code must render what the address now says.
options: A call to history.back() in the render function
A popstate listener that renders the view for the new address
Nothing; the browser should re-render automatically

questions.q: A search box updates the address with the current search term on every keystroke. Which call avoids filling the Back button with one entry per letter?
questions.explain: replaceState updates the current entry instead of adding one, so Back leaves the search page in one step.

questions.q: An SPA works when you click around, but reloading https://tasks.example/tasks/7 shows the server's 404 page. Why?
questions.explain: After a reload, the browser asks the server for the address in the bar. Static hosts have a "fallback" or "rewrite" setting that serves index.html for app routes.
options: The reload asks the server for /tasks/7, and the server has no such file; it must answer app routes with the app's HTML so the client-side router can take over

questions.q: A countdown shows "30 seconds left" and subtracts 1 in a setInterval(…, 1000). Users who switch tabs come back to a clock that is far behind. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: Counting ticks assumes each tick is exactly on time. Computing from a timestamp stays correct however late or rarely the callback runs. (requestAnimationFrame pauses completely in background tabs.)
options: setInterval is broken in all browsers; use setTimeout
Timers run after at least their delay and are slowed down in background tabs; store the end time and compute the remaining time from Date.now() on each tick
Use requestAnimationFrame, which runs in background tabs

questions.q: Why use requestAnimationFrame rather than setInterval(step, 16) for a JavaScript animation?
questions.explain: A 16 ms interval drifts against the screen's refresh and keeps running in hidden tabs. requestAnimationFrame matches the display (which may be 60, 120 or 144 Hz), so compute progress from its timestamp.
options: It runs exactly once before each repaint, in step with the screen, and pauses in hidden tabs
It runs exactly 60 times a second on every screen
It runs on a separate thread

questions.q: An animation should last 300 ms. Its step function adds 5% to a width each frame. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Frame rates differ between screens and drop when the device is busy. Progress = elapsed time ÷ duration gives the same animation everywhere.
options: The duration depends on the screen's frame rate: 20 frames take 333 ms at 60 Hz but about 167 ms at 120 Hz; compute progress from the timestamp instead

questions.q: Which statement about a Web Worker is true?
questions.explain: Workers have their own global scope. Data sent with postMessage is copied (structured clone), so neither side can change the other's objects.
options: It can read and change the page's DOM directly
It shares variables with the page
It runs on another thread with no DOM access, and exchanges copied messages with the page through postMessage
It makes every function on the page faster

questions.q: For which job is a Web Worker most worthwhile?
questions.explain: A worker pays off for heavy CPU work that would freeze the page. Waiting for the network does not block the main thread at all, and DOM work cannot be done in a worker.
options: Adding two numbers when a button is clicked
Changing the text of a heading
Parsing a 20 MB CSV file of transactions the user dropped on the page

questions.q: A notes app saves the whole document to localStorage on every keystroke, and typing feels sluggish on large notes. Why?
questions.explain: Every write blocks the thread that also handles typing. Save after the user pauses (a debounce), and consider IndexedDB, which is asynchronous, for large data.
options: localStorage sends every write to a server
localStorage is synchronous: each setItem (and the JSON.stringify before it) blocks the main thread; debounce the saves
Keys longer than 10 characters are slow

questions.q: What does new URL(userInput) do when userInput is "bello-sons.example" (no protocol)?
questions.explain: With no base URL, the text must be a complete absolute URL. Pass a base (new URL(text, location.href)) if you want relative addresses resolved.
options: It throws a TypeError, so check with URL.canParse or catch the error
It treats the text as a path on the current site

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A 404 is a normal response with ok false. Its body is readable like any other; servers often explain the error there.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The clone has its own copy of the body, so both reads work, and afterwards both bodies are used. json() parses the numbers, so they add up to 7.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A + in a query means a space. getAll returns every value of a repeated name (get would return only the first). A parameter written without a value is the empty string; a missing one is null.

questions.q: The delivery note is glued into the address with a template string. What does this print?
questions.explain: # starts the fragment, so everything after it, including &slot=evening, left the query. The slot is lost without any error. searchParams.set("note", note) would have encoded the # as %23.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A relative path replaces the last segment of the base (index.html). A leading / starts at the site's root. A query-only address keeps the whole path. A page's fetch("api/tasks") resolves the same way, which is why a missing / sends requests to the wrong place.

questions.q: This fake storage behaves like localStorage: it stores String(value). What does this print?
questions.explain: Everything is stored as a string: "3" + 1 is "31", the array became "1,2", and null became the string "null", which is not null. Only a missing key returns null. Use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON has no date type: a Date is written as an ISO string and read back as a string. Convert it yourself. getUTCMonth() counts from 0, so October is 9, plus 1 is 10.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Synchronous code first, then microtasks (promise callbacks), then timers in the order they were scheduled. Timer B was scheduled after A, inside the microtask.
options:
sync
microtask
timeout A
timeout B

timeout A
microtask
sync
timeout B

sync
timeout A
microtask
timeout B

sync
microtask
timeout B
timeout A

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The interval runs at about 10 and 20 ms, and on the second tick it cancels both itself and the 50 ms reminder, which then never runs. Cancelling timers you no longer need is part of cleaning up.
options:
bill paid after 2 checks
reminder: pay the bill

reminder: pay the bill
bill paid after 2 checks

questions.q: Messages to a worker are copied with the structured clone algorithm, which structuredClone also uses. What does this print?
questions.explain: Unlike JSON, structured clone keeps Map, Set and Date. It makes new objects (so === is false). Functions cannot be copied between threads, so they throw a DataCloneError.

questions.q: This array models a tab's history. What does it print?
questions.explain: Pushing after going back throws away the "forward" entries, exactly like a browser: after visiting /invoices, Forward can no longer reach /tasks/7.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: sort() orders the parameters by name, which gives the same query string for the same filters (useful as a cache key). The number becomes a string, and spaces are written as +.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Response.json serialises the value and sets the JSON content type for you. It is handy for fake fetch functions in tests.

questions.q: Write getJson(fetchFn, url) that calls fetchFn(url) and returns the parsed JSON, but throws Error("<url> answered <status>") for a non-ok status and Error("<url> did not return valid JSON") for a body that is not JSON. The fake fetch below plays the server.
questions.explain: Passing fetch in as a parameter lets a test use Response objects instead of a server. The await inside try matters: without it, the rejected promise from json() would escape the catch.
questions.expected:
[ { id: 1, title: 'Buy detergent' } ]
/tasks/9 answered 404
/broken did not return valid JSON

questions.q: Write productsUrl(filters) that returns https://shop.example/products with a query built by URLSearchParams: include q (trimmed) and supplier only when they are non-empty, and page only when it is above 1.
questions.explain: searchParams.set encodes & as %26 and # as %23, so the values survive. With no parameters at all, the ? is left out too.

questions.q: Write readFilter(href): parse the address, read the filter parameter, and return it only if it is "all", "open" or "done"; otherwise return "all".
questions.explain: The address is user input: anyone can type or share any query. An allow-list turns every unexpected value into the safe default. With a repeated parameter, get returns the first value.

questions.q: Write loadTasks(storage, key) for data saved as { version: 1, tasks: [...] }. Return the tasks array when the saved value parses, has version 1, and every task has a numeric id and a string title. Return [] in every other case, without throwing.
questions.explain: JSON.parse(null) returns null (it parses the text "null"), so the missing key needs the saved !== null check. An array has no version, so last year's format is refused rather than guessed at.
questions.expected:
good [ { id: 1, title: 'Buy detergent' } ]
old []
broken []
wrong []
missing []

questions.q: Version 1 of the app saved a plain array of titles. Version 2 saves { version: 2, tasks: [{ id, title, done }] }. Write migrate(saved) that returns version 2 data for either shape: number the old titles from 1 and mark them not done; return version 2 data unchanged; return null for anything else.
questions.explain: Real users keep old data for years. A migration converts each known old shape to the current one, and anything unknown (such as data from a newer version, opened in an old tab) is refused rather than overwritten.

questions.q: Write createMemoryHistory(start) returning { push(path), back(), forward(), current() }. Pushing after going back discards the forward entries, like a browser. back and forward do nothing at the ends.
questions.explain: An array plus an index is all a history is. splice(index + 1, Infinity, path) removes the forward entries and adds the new one in one step. Routing code written against this interface can be tested without a browser.

questions.q: Write safeLink(text) for a "your website" field: return the normalised address (url.href) if the text parses as a URL with protocol http: or https:, otherwise null. It must never throw.
questions.explain: An allow-list of protocols blocks javascript: links and anything unexpected. Parsing also normalises the address: the host name becomes lower case, while the path keeps its case because servers may treat it as significant.

questions.q: A flash sale's order window closes in 3 ticks. Write countdown(ticks, ms, onTick, onDone) with setInterval: call onTick with 3, 2, 1, then stop the interval and call onDone. It returns a function that cancels the countdown early.
questions.explain: Every interval needs a way to stop: when it finishes, and when the page no longer needs it. Returning a cancel function hands that control to the caller, the same idea as a view aborting its listeners.
